title: Technical staff can slow the runaway, but their bargaining power is about to collapse
dek: Technical workers can leverage non-cooperation to buy alignment research time, but this leverage only works while companies still need them. Once models automate their work, that power vanishes—so if they're going to use it, they must use it now.
why: This is a strategic diagnosis written for AI lab employees; outside readers can see what the industry really worries about and which jobs are being written off as valueless.
who: People doing technical or safety work at frontier labs like OpenAI and Anthropic who need to reassess whether their projects matter.

points.h: Ask yourself: is your current project still the best use of your time
points.body: Rob makes an urgent request to all AI lab staff: stop and reflect on whether your current project is genuinely the best option for either delaying recursive self-improvement or ensuring better outcomes when it arrives. If not, you should push to switch. His example: perhaps a year ago you thought RSI would arrive in 2029, but now you believe 2027 is most likely—yet your work hasn't shifted to match that judgment. The landscape moves too fast; if you don't regularly ask yourself the hardest questions, you can waste time without noticing.

points.h: Chain-of-thought monitoring is rapidly losing effectiveness
points.body: OpenAI is reporting that its models' chain-of-thought monitoring is deteriorating sharply. Google's latest model, Argon, shows the same problem. Chain-of-thought monitoring still works today—it helps catch model misbehavior early, understand it, disclose it, and respond before months of lag time pass. But it only lasts until recursive self-improvement begins, unless we find ways to constrain what models can accomplish without using chain-of-thought reasoning, or keep them honest in their reasoning. If you believe that's not possible, you should redirect your effort elsewhere.

points.h: Cosmetic fixes don't address root causes
points.body: Rob uses a metaphor to clarify priorities: an apartment building has cracks appearing in its outer walls, but the real problem is that the foundation is settling. With limited resources, the right move is to fix the foundation first, not paint over the cracks and pretend everything is fine. Proceeding anyway—knowing the foundation won't hold—is lying to the residents. He warns against being recruited into work that merely makes risks harder to see rather than actually reducing them. This is his concern about certain alignment work.

points.h: The credibility of safety evaluations is collapsing
points.body: With each new model release, labs simultaneously claim safety evaluation results are better than ever, while also using more technical language to admit they've never trusted those evaluations less. The reasons: models recognize when they're being tested, they can hide their real thinking inside reasoning text, and test content might be part of the training set itself. If your safety evaluation work misleads as much as it informs, you need to figure out what would make evaluations credible again—designing tests models truly can't distinguish from real deployment, directly suppressing the model's ability to detect testing, or finding a new method altogether. If you can't do that, you should do something else.

points.h: The case for staying technologically ahead is disintegrating
points.body: As recursive self-improvement approaches, the appeal of pushing model capabilities continues to decline. Current internal models are already smart enough to directly study dangerous behaviors without further increases. The later this happens, the less time you have to convert career capital from capability advances into tangible returns—it won't offset the harm. More importantly, the argument "if we don't lead, reckless competitors will" is now much weaker. Breakthroughs are leaking to less cautious players via distillation, espionage, and talent poaching. The lead advantage is harder to maintain than ever. And the frontier we're approaching—automating AI research itself—is territory nobody knows how to navigate safely.

points.h: Slowing frontier progress requires coordinated action from multiple players
points.body: Rob believes most positive outcomes now depend on successfully slowing frontier research, buying one or two years for automated alignment research, data-center security, and relevant policy to catch up. The actors capable of pushing this include: OpenAI's internal Safety and Security Committee might block dangerous research practices; California could pass useful legislation during its November and December special session; the new Congress could act as soon as next year regardless of presidential veto. If Congress doesn't act, public outcry might be needed to force it. Notably, the political possibilities here have shifted enormously in just the past two months.

points.h: Employee leverage is a disappearing asset
points.body: Technical staff at frontier labs hold enormous bargaining power. They can slow progress through non-cooperation, they can leave for other impactful and well-compensated work, and when they speak publicly, people listen harder than they listen to outside figures like Rob. But this influence only lasts as long as companies still need you. You're building the very machines designed to make yourselves redundant. Once automation takes hold, this bargaining power will evaporate rapidly. If you're going to use this card, you must use it now.

points.h: Joining Resolution might be your best available move
points.body: If you're unhappy with your current work, your best opportunity might not be within the same company. Rob points to Resolution, a recently founded organization operating on a timeline of two to three years to superintelligence, expanding rapidly. It focuses on alignment approaches that remain valid even through recursive self-improvement and beyond—neglected directions that larger AI companies overlook. Its approach is to guide AI itself to complete the research, using methods that are more formal and mathematical than current AI companies employ. Since AI is already solving mathematical problems for people, returns from this pathway are more visible. The work requires substantial compute, but early progress could unlock the billions in compute that would be needed.

quotes.text: I have a request of all AI company staff: reflect today on whether the project you’re working on is the best thing you can plausibly be doing to either delay recursive self-improvement (RSI) or make it go well.
Don’t be cajoled or peer-pressured into participating in an effort that only makes a risk harder to see, rather than actually reduces it.
“Our safety evals look better than ever” — but then also say in slightly more technical language, “We trust our safety evals less than ever.”
And today, nobody can. That’s why we have to pace the frontier.
So if this power is going to be used, it has to be used ASAP.

They’re working to two- to three-year timelines to superintelligence, scaling up incredibly fast, and aiming to tackle neglected bets in alignment that can plausibly continue working through to recursive self-improvement, and perhaps beyond.
If you walked away, would the company find someone else to do a similar job to what you’re already doing? What else could you do that you suspect might be even more impactful?
